# Technical Decisions

> **SIMULATED SCENARIO.** Velmora Coffee Roasters and all its data are fictional.

The decisions that shaped the solution, with the reason and what was given up.

## D-01 Synthetic data generated by a script, with known defects and patterns

There is no real client, so `generator/generate_data.py` plays the ERP and the finance team. It writes the
exports with the defects real exports have (duplicate customers, a missing monthly cost, returns above the
invoiced quantity, invoices dated before their order, customers without region, a messy budget workbook) and
with business patterns for the analysis to find. The same seed reproduces the same data, which makes every test
repeatable. Cost: the findings in `docs/06-insights.md` are patterns the generator was told to produce; the
exercise shows the analysis can find and measure them, not that they exist in a real company.

## D-02 Facts carry channel, region and category codes

The budget is planned by channel × region × category × month. With the codes on both facts, actuals and budget
share three small dimensions and every relationship is many-to-one and single-direction. The region stored on a
sale is the customer's current region: when a customer moves, the load reprocesses its orders, so its history
follows it (the test covers this). A point-in-time region (SCD type 2) was not requested.

## D-03 Incremental load by affected order, applied with MERGE

Revenue on an order line depends on six source tables. Instead of tracking each table's changes separately in
the facts, the procedure finds the orders touched by any change since the last run and rebuilds their rows,
applying them with `MERGE` (update only when a value differs). This keeps one code path for incremental and full
loads and makes the test simple: a full reload after an incremental one must find nothing to change. Cost: a
product rename or a standard cost correction reprocesses many orders (8,523 in the test, about 4 % of history),
which is acceptable at this volume.

## D-04 Source loader in Python, not PowerShell

The first loader converted each CSV value in PowerShell and took 580 s for 950,000 rows. The Python loader with
`pyodbc` `fast_executemany` takes 22 s for the same files. The generator was already Python, so the build needs
no new runtime. Deployment of the SQL scripts stayed in PowerShell with the .NET client: it runs the scripts with
`QUOTED_IDENTIFIER ON` without needing `sqlcmd`.

## D-05 Budget prepared in Power Query, with an explicit category mapping

Rule R7 asks for the workbook to be prepared in Power Query. A staging query unpivots every sheet; the Budget
table skips titles and the Total row, upper-cases regions and maps category names through an inline table that
includes the misspellings found in past workbooks. Mapping through the SQL category table was avoided because
combining the Excel and SQL sources in one query brings Power Query's privacy-level rules into play. An unknown
category name is not dropped: it stays unmapped and the `Unmapped Budget Rows` measure counts it. The workbook's
own Total rows are kept in a support table to prove that the prepared budget lost nothing.

## D-06 Budget measures blank outside the budget grain

The budget has no customer or product. Showing the total budget next to one customer's revenue would be wrong,
so budget measures return blank when customers, products or sales attributes are filtered.

## D-07 Model and report written as code

`powerbi/generate_model.py` writes the TMDL and `powerbi/build_report.py` builds every page with the `pbir` CLI,
so both can be rebuilt and reviewed in a diff. Lineage tags are uuid5 of the object path, so regenerating gives
identical files; after a save in Power BI Desktop the model files were byte-identical to the generator output.
Cost: a change made by hand in Desktop is lost at the next build unless it is copied into the script.

## D-08 Report fixes found only by rendering

Validation of the PBIR files passed while the rendered report was wrong in four places, each fixed in the build
script:
- `pbir` writes categorical filter values as text, which never matches the integer year; the year filter is an
  Advanced filter, which keeps the integer literal.
- Charts sort by value by default; month axes are sorted by the month column.
- The KPI visual shows the last point of its trend axis (December), not the year; the headline row uses cards.
- A table grouped customers by name, adding up different customers with the same name in different cities
  (36,508 customers, 36,184 distinct names); the table and its Top 15 filter use the customer id.

## D-09 Reserved words

`LineNo` is a T-SQL keyword, so the line columns are `LineNumber` and `CreditLineNumber` in the generator and
the database. `powerbi/validate_model.ps1` rejects DAX variables named with reserved words (`Before`, `Top` and
similar), which the TMDL parser accepts but break the measure when the model loads.

## D-10 Policy and promotion flags computed in the load, from reference tables

The discount policy check (CR-01) and the promotion period (CR-03) are computed by `etl.usp_LoadSales` and stored
on each sales row, so the measures only add and divide. The rule needs the customer's segment, the policy table
and the order's campaign; doing it in DAX would mean a row-by-row lookup over 500,000 rows at query time. The
promotion calendar became a reference table (`ref.Promotion`) because the ERP stamps a campaign code on the orders
but not the category the promotion funds. Cost: reference tables have no timestamps, so a policy or calendar change
needs a full reload.

## D-11 Margin bridge in DAX, checked against SQL

The bridge (CR-02) follows the report filters: by channel, region or category it explains that slice's margin,
which a stored table of company-level contributions could not do. It is one measure over a six-row step table,
iterating product × channel cells of the selected year and the previous one. `validation/validate_kpis.ps1`
compares every step for 2024 and 2025 with `analysis/margin_bridge.sql`, written independently in SQL.
`Cells` turned out to be a reserved word in DAX: the first version failed after loading and the variable was
renamed; `powerbi/validate_model.ps1` now rejects it offline.

## D-12 A design of its own ("Velmora Roast")

The first build reused the layout of the previous portfolio project (default theme, page buttons along the top).
The report now has its own identity: an espresso navigation rail on the left with the brand and one button per
page, a cream canvas, caramel for actual values and slate blue for the comparison series (budget, prior year),
terracotta for negatives. A warm beige was tried first as the comparison colour and rejected: next to caramel it
fails the normal-vision and colour-blind separation checks of the dataviz palette validator. The six data colours
pass all its checks. The rail uses buttons because `pbir` cannot make the page navigator vertical; each button
targets the page id, since Power BI ignores display names in navigation actions. Formatting goes in the theme
where it renders (colours, fonts, solid bars, no area shading, no title or border on buttons); the fill and text
of buttons and shapes are set on each visual, because theme defaults did not reach them in Power BI Desktop. The
report build takes about ten minutes as a result.
